title: Claude Made It: Vibe-Coded Mods and the Backlash
description: Why "Claude made it" became a meme, what the vibe-coding backlash is actually about, and how to ship AI-assisted mods people won't hate.
author: freellm.site
content:
"Claude made it" is the punchline of a joke about how much software now ships with an AI assistant's fingerprints on it (game mods, RuneLite plugins, Godot projects, Discord bots) and how obvious that is to everyone who downloads it. The meme doesn't say Claude the model is bad. It mocks a specific pattern: a tool built in an afternoon, announced with em-dashes and rocket emojis, hammering someone else's API, and shipped by an author who can't answer questions about their own code.

![Claude Made It: Vibe-Coded Mods and the Backlash](/images/blog/claude-made-it-vibe-coded-mods/image-0.jpg)

If you came here from the meme and want the practical version, read on for what the community complaints say, which ones are fair, and how to use Claude (or any assistant) on a mod or plugin without becoming the joke.

## Where the meme came from

Three things happening at once explain it.

The first is **volume**. A player in the Old School RuneScape community shipped a RuneLite plugin whose whole purpose was generating more plugins from inside the game: you type what you want, the assistant asks follow-up questions, and code appears. The top reply joked that it didn't use *enough* of the community wiki's bandwidth and should be scrapped and rebuilt worse. Another called it recursive self-improvement. The author's own follow-up, that he doesn't write the code, he just promotes it, is the line the meme is really about.

The second is **the tells**. People now recognise AI-written release notes on sight: bolded feature headers, "Great question! 🤔", a breathless changelog for a weekend project. Fairly or not, that style has come to mean "nobody read this before it shipped."

The third is **a loop everyone has lived through**. The most-upvoted comparison in the thread was ordering a Big Mac and getting a cheeseburger, then a chicken sandwich, then an apology and another wrong item, each delivered with total confidence and a cheerful correction. That's what debugging a model that doesn't know what it doesn't know feels like, and it's why "Claude made it" reads as an accusation rather than a credit.

The loudest comment in the original thread wasn't anti-AI. It argued that AI is a tool with legitimate uses, and the problem starts only when most of the end product was made *by* the tool rather than *with* it. That's where the community is drawing the line, and it's a reasonable place to draw it.

## What the meme gets wrong

The same week, Anthropic published research in which Claude worked out the origin of the NSA's P-curve seeds, a question that had been open for roughly 25 years. The model's own reaction was to suspect it had made a mistake, because surely something that obvious would have been found already. ([Anthropic's writeup is here.](https://www.anthropic.com/research/ecdsa-curve-origins))

The most useful comment on that thread deflated the hype accurately. The answer turned out to be astonishingly simple, and it had been overlooked *because* people assumed anything from the NSA must be complicated or backdoored. Claude didn't invent new mathematics. It quickly tested the boring hypothesis nobody had bothered with.

That's an accurate picture of what these models can do. They're excellent at exhaustively trying obvious things, writing boilerplate and turning intent into syntax. They're bad at noticing when the obvious thing is wrong, which is exactly the skill a mod author needs when their plugin starts making 400 requests a minute to a volunteer-run wiki.

## What people are angry about

Without the jokes, the complaints are specific and fixable:

| Complaint | What's underneath it | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| "Doesn't use enough of the wiki's bandwidth" | AI-generated code fetches naively: no cache, no backoff, no rate limit | Cache aggressively, respect rate limits, identify your client |
| "Ask Claude, I just promote it" | Author can't maintain or debug what they shipped | Read every line you ship; you own the bug reports |
| The Big Mac loop | Confident wrong output accepted without verification | Tests before merge, not vibes |
| AI-styled release notes | Signals the human skipped review | Write your own README in your own voice |
| "More than 50% made *by* AI" | Attribution and effort transparency | Say what was generated and what you reviewed |
| "Where the hell did my Godot go" | Generated changes sprawling across a project | Small diffs, version control, one concern per commit |

None of this is anti-AI; it's the review standard any contribution faces. For the hiring version of the same standard, see [AI Engineer Interviews: How to Test AI-Assisted Coding](/blog/ai-engineer-interview-ai-assisted-coding/). Its evaluation criteria map almost exactly onto "is this mod maintainable?"

![Developer reviewing a code diff on a monitor with a small painted rock sitting beside the keyboard](/images/blog/claude-made-it-vibe-coded-mods/image-1.jpg)
*Photo: [Developer Satisfaction Survey - 2020 - Code Review - important to work](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=90638476) by Greg (WMF), CC BY-SA*

## Fixing the bandwidth complaint

The most common real harm from vibe-coded mods is hammering a community API. Assistants write the simplest possible fetch because that's what the prompt asked for. Wrap at least this around any external call in a plugin or bot: a cache, backoff, and a real User-Agent so maintainers can contact you instead of banning your tool outright.

```python
import time
import random
import requests
from functools import lru_cache

SESSION = requests.Session()
SESSION.headers["User-Agent"] = (
    "MyPlugin/1.0 (https://github.com/me/myplugin; me@example.com)"
)

MIN_INTERVAL = 1.0  # seconds between requests to the same host
_last_call = 0.0

def _throttle():
    global _last_call
    wait = MIN_INTERVAL - (time.monotonic() - _last_call)
    if wait > 0:
        time.sleep(wait)
    _last_call = time.monotonic()

@lru_cache(maxsize=2048)  # same key is never fetched twice per process
def fetch_json(url: str, attempts: int = 4) -> dict:
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        _throttle()
        resp = SESSION.get(url, timeout=10)

        if resp.status_code == 429 or resp.status_code >= 500:
            retry_after = resp.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = (
                float(retry_after)
                if retry_after
                else (2 ** attempt) + random.random()
            )
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue

        resp.raise_for_status()
        return resp.json()

    raise RuntimeError(f"gave up after {attempts} attempts: {url}")
```

Three properties matter here, and an assistant will usually skip all of them unless you ask. The `lru_cache` makes repeated lookups free. The `Retry-After` handling backs off when the server says so instead of retrying in a tight loop. And the contactable User-Agent lets a maintainer email you instead of blocking your whole plugin. For long-running mods, persist the cache to disk instead of keeping it in memory.

## Using Claude on a mod without becoming the joke

A workflow that holds up:

### 1. Own the architecture, delegate the typing
Decide the file layout, the data flow and where external calls happen yourself, and hand over the mechanical parts. In every failure the meme mocks, the model chose the architecture.

### 2. Keep diffs reviewable
Ask for one change at a time. Nobody can review a 900-line generated patch, and "where did my project go" is what follows. Commit between steps so you can always get back.

### 3. Make it test the boring hypothesis
Copy the ECDSA approach: ask the model to list the simple explanations before the clever ones and to say what would disprove each. That's where these models are strongest.

### 4. Write tests before you believe anything
The Big Mac loop ends as soon as you have an assertion instead of a feeling. One runnable check per non-trivial behaviour is enough.

### 5. Write your own release notes
If your announcement reads as generated, people will assume the code was too. Say plainly what the plugin does, what was generated and what you reviewed.

### 6. Don't run an agent against someone else's service unsupervised
An agent with network access and no rate limiting is a load generator. If it takes actions with real consequences, accountability is a live question; see [Who Is Liable When an AI Agent Breaks the Law?](/blog/who-is-liable-when-ai-agents-break-the-law/) and the [FTC's position that developers are liable for their agents' conduct](/blog/ftc-ai-agent-liability-developers/).

## On naming your tools after your tools

One of the better side threads asked: *is anyone actually named Claude?* Yes. It's an ordinary first name that plenty of real people have, including people in the crew credits of shows the thread went digging through. Many assume the name refers to Claude Shannon and information theory, but Anthropic hasn't published an official naming story, so treat that as folklore.

Another thread had someone ask Claude who it would hire, get the answer "a rock," draw a face on one, and be told the rock had perfect attendance. It illustrates a real effect better than it seems to. The model produced a bit consistent with the persona, the person played along, and each reinforced the other. That mirroring is well documented; [Why ChatGPT Sounds Like You: The Mirror Effect](/blog/why-chatgpt-sounds-like-you/) explains the mechanism. With a rock it's harmless. It's less harmless when what gets mirrored back to you is "yes, this code is correct."

## If you want to try this without paying

You don't need a paid plan for the workflow above. Several providers offer free tiers you can point an editor or agent at, and most speak the OpenAI wire format, so switching models is a base-URL change. Start with [Best Free LLM APIs for Coding in 2026](/blog/best-free-llm-apis-for-coding/) and [Use a Free LLM API in Cursor, Claude Code, or Any AI Tool](/blog/use-free-llm-api-cursor-claude-code/). Claude's pricing, rate limits and model availability change often, so check [Anthropic's documentation](https://docs.anthropic.com/) instead of any blog's numbers.

## FAQ

### Is "Claude made it" an insult?
It's usually aimed at how something was shipped, not at the model: unreviewed code, generated release notes, and an author who can't answer questions about their own project. People who use the same tool carefully don't get the joke pointed at them.

### Did Claude really solve a 25-year-old cryptography mystery?
Anthropic published research in which Claude identified the origin of the NSA's ECDSA curve seeds, a question open for about 25 years. The community's caveat matters: the answer was simple and had been overlooked because people assumed it had to be complex. Read [Anthropic's writeup](https://www.anthropic.com/research/ecdsa-curve-origins) for what was and wasn't done.

### How much AI-generated code is "too much" in an open-source mod?
There's no official threshold. The rule of thumb from the thread is that the tool becomes a problem when the model produced most of the product and the author didn't review it. The practical test is whether you can debug and maintain it.

### What's the most common technical problem with vibe-coded plugins?
Naive network calls with no caching, no backoff, no rate limiting and no identifying User-Agent, which is why community wikis and APIs get hit hard. The snippet above fixes that in about thirty lines.

### Is anyone actually named Claude?
Yes, it's a common first name. The popular link to Claude Shannon is an assumption, not a documented naming decision by Anthropic.
